segments.say: If someone had walked into Hana's bedroom ten minutes ago and spoken to her, she might not have heard them. The lamp, the room, the time, her alarm at half past six, all of it had faded. She was somewhere else, in a cold harbor town where the woman in her book was about to open a letter. That feeling, of being carried away into a story, has a name in psychology. It's called narrative transportation.

The idea was developed by the psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock. They described transportation as a kind of mental journey. Your attention, your imagination and your feelings all become focused on the events of the story. The real world fades a little. And, importantly, they suggested that people may return from that journey changed in some small way.

In a set of studies published in 2000, Green and Brock asked people to read a short, emotional story about a young girl who is attacked by a psychiatric patient at a shopping mall. Afterward, people answered questions about how transported they had felt, and about their beliefs on related topics, such as how safe public places are.

show.what: People read a short story about a young girl attacked at a shopping mall. Readers who were more transported into the story held beliefs more in line with the story afterward, and spotted fewer false notes in it.

segments.say: To measure transportation, they asked questions like these. While reading, could you picture the events happening? Were you mentally involved in the story? Did you want to learn how it ended? Did you find yourself thinking about what might have happened differently? People who agreed strongly were considered more transported.

What they found was that the more transported people felt, the more their beliefs tended to match the story. Highly transported readers were more likely to agree with views the story seemed to suggest. They also felt more positively about the girl in the story. Their minds had travelled further, and come back carrying more of the story with them.

Here's the part that surprises many people. In some of the studies, the story was described to some readers as a true news report, and to others as fiction. You might expect that knowing it was invented would protect people from being influenced. But in their results, the label made little difference to the effect of transportation. A transported mind seemed to take the story in, whatever it had been told about where the story came from.

They also tried something clever. They asked readers to circle any parts of the story that struck them as false, or that didn't ring true. Researchers sometimes call this Pinocchio circling. Highly transported readers circled fewer false notes. When you're deep inside a story, the inner critic, the part of you that checks and questions, seems to fall a little quieter.

Why might that be? One explanation is simple. When you're absorbed in a story, your attention is busy with the events and the characters. There's less attention left over for arguing back. And you're not being told what to think in so many words. You're being shown. And it's hard to argue with something you've seen.

show.text: When you are inside a story, it is harder to argue with it.

segments.say: This is part of why stories have such power in every area of life, from charity appeals to health campaigns to political speeches. A careful set of statistics often invites us to check the numbers. A single, vivid story often invites us to feel. And researchers who study health communication have explored using stories for exactly this reason, to help people take in messages that might otherwise bounce off.

None of this means stories are a trick, or that being moved by them is foolish. Being transported is one of the great pleasures of life. It's part of how we learn about places we've never been, and lives we'll never live. But it does mean stories carry a kind of quiet authority. We tend to believe them a little more than we realize.

So here's what transportation seems to do. It focuses our attention and feelings on the story. It lets the real world fade for a while. It can move our beliefs toward the story's view. And it seems to quiet our inner critic.

So if a story ever seems to be changing your mind about something important, there's a gentle way to protect yourself without spoiling the pleasure. Enjoy the story fully. Then, afterward, step out of it and ask a few quiet questions. Is this one case typical? What would the numbers say? Was the story built to make me feel a certain way?

Hana, when she finally closes her book tonight, will carry a little of that cold harbor town back with her. Perhaps a feeling about letters, or about the sea, or about a kind of person. Most of that will be harmless, even good. That's part of why we read. It's simply worth knowing that the journey works both ways.

But we still haven't answered the question that's keeping Hana awake. Why is it so hard to stop? Why does a story make us need to know what happens next, even when we're tired, even when we're not sure we like it? There are a few ideas about that, and one of them involves a curious feeling psychologists describe as an information gap.

show.cap: Why we can't put it down

segments.say: Before we get there, though, there's one more thing about stories and belief worth exploring. Because stories don't only feel gripping. Rich, detailed stories can also feel more likely to be true. And that can lead even very clever people into a surprising mistake.
To see it, we'll meet a famous imaginary woman named Linda, and then sit in on some imaginary juries. Both, it turns out, show the same quiet power of a good story to feel convincing.
